The orphan receptor GPR88 is a G protein-coupled receptor with robust expression in the striatum of the brain. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that GPR88 is implicated in mediation of dopaminergic activity and plays an important role in striatal functions. In this project, we synthesized and characterized two GPR88 radioligands, which are powerful tools for mechanistic and cell-based ligand-receptor interaction studies of this novel receptor.  

Our main achievements are: (1) We have successfully developed synthetic methods and prepared two radioligands [3H]RTI-33 and [3H]RTI-192 with high HPLC chemical purity and specific activity; (2)	We have characterized [3H]RTI-33 by both saturation binding and competition binding studies using filtration assays in membranes prepared from stable hGPR88-CHO cells, as well as in mouse striatal membranes endogenously expressing GPR88; and (3) We have published one paper and submitted a manuscript to summarize our main findings in peer-reviewed journals.

The major findings are:
i.	Despite predictions, CALHM4 does not function as an ion channel under the conditions in which CALHM1 and CALHM1/3 can be shown to function.  Thus, either CALHM4 is not an ion channel, or, 
        more likely, conditions remain to be identified to activate it.

ii.	CALHM6 expression is toxic in oocytes. It is localized to the plasma membrane and it generates “leak” currents. Nevertheless, the ion currents recorded are small. We hypothesize that the large pore 
        of CALHM6, which is bigger than that of CALHM1, may cause leak of critical cytoplasmic components necessary for cell health. The small currents suggest that, similar to CALHM4, conditions to 
        activate the channel more fully remain to be identified.

iii.	CALHM5 appears to be a bone-fide ion channel with properties distinct from those of CALHM1 and CALHM1/3. But what cell types and what role these currents play remain to be discovered. 

The functions of the CALHM family remain enigmatic. Our studies have discovered a new ion channel in CALHM5, but we lack information about where it is expressed in the body. CALHMs 2 and 4 structurally resemble CALHM1 but their expression does not generate ion currents. CALHM6 has been shown to function in immunity, but whether it does so as an ion channel or by other mechanisms remains to be determined.

This grant made progress in studying a currently understudied type of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) known as ADGRB3 (a.k.a. BAI3). GPCRs are noteworthy because they are a type of protein commonly targeted by pharmaceuticals to treat a wide variety of maladies. Mutations in the human ADGRB3 gene are linked to both neuropsychiatric diseases and cancers, suggesting this gene is a high value therapeutic target. However, no mechanistic explanations regarding ADGRB3 function have been proposed to explain these genetic associations. This grant succeeded in developing novel tools to assist in the research of ADGRB3. Proteins of the C1QL family are known ligands and likely activators of this GPCR. We have created novel genetically modified mouse lines that were engineered to have ‘tags’ on the proteins which will facilitate future research on both where and how these protein-protein interactions occur. The future research will be significant because it will form the etiological and biochemical foundation for subsequent research on disorders of ADGRB3 signaling, and demonstrate which cellular contexts/diseases might benefit from a small molecule drug targeting the ADGRB3-C1QL protein binding interface.

Specific patterns of action potential firing in neurons are critical for transmitting information. Action potential firing is regulated in part by the expression of different ion channels on the cell surface. Though some of these ion channels are well-studied, others have been more difficult to investigate because we lack specific drugs that can be used to activate or inactivate them. Here we used a DNA editing tool called CRISPR to mutate genes encoding specific ion channel subunits in dopamine neurons in mice and measured what happens to action potential waveforms and firing patterns.

Using this approach we studied the function of the auxiliary potassium channel subunit Kcanb2 (Kvbeta2). When we used CRISPR to "knock out" this gene we saw that the shape of the action potential changed and the action potential firing pattern in dopamine neurons became more irregular. We discovered that this was a result of reduced trafficking of Kv1-type potassium channels to the cell surface as well as a shift in the gating properties of those channels. When we used CRISPR to knock out the gene Kcna2, which encodes a pore-forming Kv1 subunit, we saw similar effects on dopamine neuron firing properties.

These results show that Kv1 potassium channels are important regulators of dopamine neuron activity, and that their trafficking and function is impacted in these neurons by interactions with auxiliary subunits. We also showed that viral-based CRISPR approaches are an effective means of studying ion channels that have previously been difficult to investigate.

The present R03 project significantly contributed to identify novel drug targets to overcome hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) metastasis and therapy resistance. Specifically, we identified two understudied protein kinases, i.e., STK17A and B that control HCC cell resistance to targeted therapy. Pharmacological inhibitors for these kinases are available, and in future research we will use these inhibitors to validate that STK17A and B may represent valuable drug targets in vivo. Furthermore, in lieu if studying STK17A and B, we have developed a novel bioanalytical platform to study the dysregulation of kinase interaction networks in high throughput (Golkowski et al., Molecular Cell, 2023). Collectively our results greatly expand our understanding of understudied kinase functions in cancer, and delivered novel bioanalytical tool that will transform cell signaling and cancer reserach.

In this study, we examined the role of HCAR1 in BAT in the control of body weight and glucose homeostasis. Specifically, we overexpressed HCAR1 in iBAT of male C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat diet. We found that overexpression of these receptors significantly upregulated the thermogenic gene expression in BAT associated with increased iBAT temperature. Mice overexpressing HCAR1 in iBAT were protected from DIO and displayed improved glucose and insulin tolerance.
These were some of our main findings:
•BATHCAR1 male mice were protected from DIO. This may be attributed in part to increased thermogenesis in iBAT.
•BATHCAR1 male mice exhibited improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity compared to the control group on high fat feeding. This appears to be attributed in part to lower levels of plasma insulin and leptin in BATHCAR1 mice.
•In contrast to the antilipolytic effect of HACR1 in white adipocytes, BATHCAR1 mice did not exhibit changes in plasma glycerol concentrations compared to the control group.
•Genetic knockdown of Gq proteins in BAT of BATHCAR1 mice abolished the anti-obesity effect. Thus, HCAR1 in BAT appears to be coupled to Gq proteins.
•Our results provide novel insights into the role of lactate and its cognate receptors in the control of energy balance and glucose homeostasis.

Over the course of this award, we showed GBM cell-lines exhibiting VRK2 promoter methylation are more dependent on its paralog, VRK1. We initiated mechanistic studies to find putative substrates and identify the cause of cell death in cells lacking both VRK1 and VRK2. Taken together, our results credential VRK1 as a viable target for VRK2-methylated GBM and indicate the reduced cell viability in cells lacking VRK1 and VRK2 is due to disruption of normal post-mitotic barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF) function. Our studies suggest targeting VRK1 in GBM with methylation at the VRK2 gene promoter is a potential therapeutic strategy. We are preparing a manuscript describing these results for submission.

In this project, we have made several findings to delineate the relationship between p21 Protein-Activated Kinase 3 (PAK3) and one of its upstream regulator, neural developmentally down-regulated gene 4-like (Nedd4-2, also known as Nedd4L). Because Nedd4-2 is encoded by an epilepsy-associated gene and we have shown that Nedd4-2 mediates epilepsy-associated cognitive behavior, linking Nedd4-2 to PAK3 is critical to further understand cognition-associated neuronal plasticity.

The first discovery we made is that we confirmed PAK3 as a substrate of the long isoform but not short isoform of Nedd4-2. This is important because the long isoform of Nedd4-2 is likely involved more with epilepsy based on our previous studies. Because single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in human Nedd4-2 lead to differential expression of these two isoforms, our findings also suggest that Nedd4-2-dependnet ubiquitination on PAK3 are likely regulated differentially on different populations. 

The second discovery we made is that, among the three currently known epilepsy-associated missense mutations of Nedd4-2, the serine-233 to leucine (S233L) mutation impacted the ubiquitination of PAK3 the most. This observation suggest several new findings. First, it suggests that, despite all three mutations occur near the substrate binding region of Nedd4-2, the effects on individual substrates are likely different. Second, it suggests that S233L mutation may affect PAK3-associated neuronal plasticity the most. Lastly, it suggests that epilepsy-associated cognitive impairment is complex even with the dysregulation on the same protein. 

In summary, we have made the molecular connection between PAK3 and Nedd4-2 in regards to epilepsy. As a future direction, we plan to explore how such regulation may affect neuronal plasticity and memory behavior in vivo.

As we reported, we have made critical progresses to achieve the goals of the proposal. 

First, we have generated animal models to determine the expression pattern of Gpr162 in the hypothalamus and functional relevance for metabolic regulation. We verified the GFP expression in the Gpr162-F2A-GFP mice that will mark endogenous Gpr162 expression in the brain. We’ll further characterize the cell types that express Gpr162. Moreover, we have generated the AgRP neuron specific Gpr162 conditional knockout animals (KO). We did metabolic profiling and found the KO had reduced food intake during nighttime when the rodents are most actively engaged in feeding. We will examine Gpr162 function in other hypothalamic neurons, such as POMC neurons, by generating neuron type specific Gpr162 conditional knockout animals. With these experiments successfully completed, we will determine Gpr162 expression pattern in the brain and decipher the metabolic function of this GPCR.

Secondly, we have acquired the the PathHunter β-Arrestin Orphan GPCR cell line (GPCR 162) from DiscoverX. These cells are engineered to co-express the ProLinkTM (PK) tagged GPCR and the Enzyme Acceptor (EA) tagged β-Arrestin. Activation of the GPCR-PK induces β-Arrestin-EA recruitment, forcing complementation of the β-galactosidase enzyme fragments (EA and PK). The resulting functional enzyme hydrolyzes substrate to generate a chemiluminescent signal representing agonist activity. We subsequently developed and validated an approach for chemical compound screening to search for agonists of GPR162-stimulated β-Arrestin recruitment. We screened 7,100 compounds in the CNS library from LifeChemicals where in addition to containing targeted diverse scaffolds, compounds are designed to exhibit increased blood brain barrier permeability. From the primary screen, we selected 25 compounds with diverse structures that showed a 5-8 times higher luminescent signal (i.e. presumably β-Arrestin recruitment) when compared to control (vehicle). We then purchased powders for each of these 25 compounds for confirmation testing. One compound was excluded due to solubility, and the remaining 24 compounds were evaluated in the GPR162 β-Arrestin assay using four different concentrations (30 µM, 10 µM, 3 µM and 1 µM) on at least three individual occasions. Unfortunately, all 24 compounds failed to robustly stimulate β-Arrestin recruitment. The top 14 compounds revealed a very modest luminescent increase compared to control that was only approximately ~ 10% higher. Despite the modest signal, the activity of the selected 14 compounds was also tested in a cyclic AMP assay at 20 µM and 60 µM. As anticipated, no compound-mediated change in cyclic AMP accumulation was observed (n=2). The results of our screening efforts were similar to that from Dr. Roth’s laboratory in that they also failed to identify agonist for GPR162. Despite our results, we firmly believe that a much larger scale screening effort for ligands for GPR162 would identify the first ever GPR162 agonists.  

We will disseminate the research results to the scientific community by publication and data repository. We will choose to publish in Open Access journals for better public accessibility. Other reagents generated with the funding will be accessible to the scientific community as well. 

With the support of this R03 award and the joint efforts of two PIs with complementary expertise in metabolism research and GPCR molecular pharmacology, we plan to report our findings in the current R03 award in primary research articles. We also plan to compete for additional funding, such as NIH R01.

Patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) display severe anemia but the mechanisms underlying this phenotype are incompletely understood. Right open reading frame kinase 2 (RIOK2) is a protein kinase located at 5q15, a region frequently lost in MDS del(5q) patients. Here, we show that 50% reduction in Riok2 expression resulted in reduced red blood cell (RBC) production leading to anemia. Furthermore, analysis of multiple patient-derived loss-of-function RIOK2 mutations showed marked attenuation of RBC development. Systematic analysis of Riok2-deficient mice identified an important role for an immune cell-derived protein interleukin-22 (IL-22) in driving the anemia. Neutralizing IL-22 signaling alleviated induced-anemia not only in Riok2-deficient mice but also in wild-type mice. Levels of IL-22 were increased in del(5q) MDS patients suggesting that IL-22 inhibition presents a therapeutic opportunity for MDS. Importantly, retrospective analysis of data from a clinical trial analyzing the efficacy of anti-IL-22 in arthritis revealed a significant increase in hemoglobin in the anti-IL-22-administered group compared to the placebo group. This work reveals a possible therapeutic opportunity for reversing many stress-induced anemias (MDS, chronic kidney disease, chronic inflammation, chemotherapy-induced) by targeting IL-22 signaling. We are currently in late-stage discussions with the private sector to move toward a first-in-class clinical trial of a human IL22 antibody to alleviate anemia in MDS patients.

The purpose of the project was to develop cell lines useful in testing the idea that signaling through the GPR31 receptor (a high affinity 12-S-HETE receptor) affects KRAS trafficking and/or signaling.  KRAS is an important oncogene involved in 20% of cancers such that information on its trafficking and signaling would be useful in developing novel anticancer drugs.  To accomplish our goal, we required a cell line that stably expresses GPR31.  Although we were successful in expressing GPR31 transiently in several different cell types, we were unable to make a cell line stably expressing the receptor despite employing a variety of state-of-the-art approaches.  The reason for this failure is not clear and solving the technical problem will take several more months of experimentation, well beyond the funding period.  Accordingly, our studies remain incomplete.

We have established a comprehensive structure-activity relationship (SAR) of Neuropeptide B (NPB) and identified a peptidomimetic ([desaminoTrp1]WYKXXXGRAAGLL-NH2) that has equivalent nanomolar potency as the endogenous peptides but with significantly enhanced metabolic stability against rat plasma (39.1 min vs. 11.9 min). We will share this ligand with research community upon request.

We have disseminated these results via publications and scientific presentations listed below.
Nguyen, T.; Decker, A.M.; Snyder, R.W.; Tonetti, E.C.; Gamage, T.F.; Zhang, Y. Neuropeptide B/W receptor 1 peptidomimetic agonists: Structure-activity relationships and plasma stability. Eur. J. Med. Chem., 2022, 231, 114149.
Nguyen, T.; Decker, A.M.; Snyder, R.; Tonetti, E.; Barrus, D.; Gamage, T.; Zhang, Y.(2022, Mar) Development of Neuropeptide B/W peptidomimetic agonists. Poster presented at the virtual Illuminating the Druggable Genome.

Diabetes in its many forms is a disorder of glucose homeostasis that afflicts nearly half a billion individuals world-wide.  The dysfunction and/or loss of the insulin-producing islet β-cell are central in the transition from impaired glucose tolerance to frank diabetes in virtually all forms of diabetes.  Over the past decade, our laboratory has focused on inflammation and the cellular response to inflammation as a central mechanism that contributes to β-cell dysfunction and death in both type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D). GPR31 has recently been de-orphaned and identified as the 12(S)-HETE receptor. We have generated congenic Gpr31b-/- mice on the C57BL6/J background through traditional ES cell cloning. These mice are viable and exhibit normal growth and glucose tolerance at 8 and 12 weeks of age in both males and female. Using multiple low dose streptozotocin, a model of type 1 diabetes, wildtype mice became hyperglycemic, while Gpr31b-/- mice remained normal glycemic suggesting knockout of Gpr31b results, at least in part, in protection of the β cell. Upon ex vivo treatment with pro-inflammatory cytokines, Gpr31b-/- islets differentially express genes that when subjected to GO pathway analysis resulted in alterations to immunity, oxidative stress, ER stress, and MAPK activity/binding pathways. Together, these data suggest that GPR31 is a potential target for prevention of β-cell dysfunction and type 1 diabetes.

Outcomes

Project: Biochemical approaches to enlighten GPR85 function
PI: Aashish Manglik, M.D., Ph.D.
Organization: University of California, San Francisco

Cells use hundreds of individual G protein-coupled receptors as “channels” to send and receive information. While the messages for many receptors are now known, over 100 receptors remain orphan: we don’t know what messages they respond to. One such receptor is GPR85, which is hypothesized to be important in the development of the nervous system and is linked to learning, memory, and neuropsychiatric diseases like schizophrenia. We set out to understand what GPR85 responds to.

In this project, we developed new approaches to purify GPR85 to enable a detailed biochemical study of this receptor. 

Our main findings were:
1)	A new approach that allows us to purify milligram quantities of GPR85. A similar approach may allow us and other scientists to purify other orphan receptors.
2)	Discovery of a new lipid molecule that is bound to GPR85. This may provide the first clues into how GPR85 works.

Project: “Characterization of an Understudied Kinase, NEK5, in Acquisition of a Mesenchymal and Migratory Cell Phenotype.”
Contact PI: Burow, Matthew E.
Organization: Tulane University

The overarching objective of this proposal is to identify a potent, selective, and cell active NEK5 inhibitor, and to assess the roles of NEK5 breast cancer signaling. 

Medicinal Chemistry for NEK5 
We utilized iterative medicinal chemistry around a promising pyrimidine scaffold to generate a high-quality chemical probe of the understudied kinase NEK5. Through this, we identified a scaffold with overlapping and selective NEK 3, 5, 9 inhibitory activity. From this and other probes, a scaffold targeted selectively against other kinases was identified. 

Biological Role for NEK5.  We utilized a combination of overexpression and shRNA-knock-down strategies to define a role for NEK5 expression in breast cancer cell systems. Overexpression of  NEK5 results in the promotion of a more in vitro invasive and in vivo metastatic phenotype in lumina breast cancer cells, which coordinates with acquiring a partial EMT-like phenotype and gene expression changes.  Knock-down of NEK5 expression in TNBC and metaplastic breast cancer cells resulted in decreased motility/invasive phenotype and partial suppression of the metastatic phenotype.  

Overall, these findings suggest that NEK5 may exert a role in cancer cell tumorigenesis, metastasis, and potentially regulation of therapeutic response or resistance. The development of novel chemical probes for NEK5 also offers the potential to further the interrogation of this pathway in cancer subtypes. It provides a path towards translation of NEK5 targeting in the clinical setting.

The kinase Tau tubulin kinase 2 (TTBK2) is essential for the formation of primary cilia- vital signaling organelles important in development and disease. Mutations in the gene encoding this kinase result in the production of a truncated protein. These mutations are associated with a dominantly inherited neurodegenerative condition in humans-spinocerebellar ataxia type 11 (SCA11). We have shown that while the disease-associated truncations can’t traffic to the correct area in a cell to mediate assembly of cilia, they also dominantly interfere with the ability of the full length TTBK2 to assemble cilia. However, full length TTBK2 and the SCA11-associated truncation do not physically interact, so the molecular mechanism by which the truncations interfere with cilia function was unknown. 

To better understand how these SCA11 truncations interfere with cilia formation and therefore the cellular basis of this human disease, we performed a screen to identify proteins that interact with the SCA11 variants of TTBK2 compared with full length TTBK2.

Our key findings were:
•	Full length TTBK2 interacts with numerous proteins at the centrosome, which templates the cilium, as well as other proteins that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics.
•	The SCA11-associated truncated form of TTBK2 loses these interactions, and instead interacts with peroxisomal proteins and specific actin cytoskeleton regulators.
•	The SCA11-associated truncations localize to peroxisomes- organelle important for the trafficking and metabolism of lipids as well as reactive oxygen species in cells.
•	Expression of these proteins in human cells alters the number and shape of peroxisomes.
•	This may affect the trafficking of key lipids to cilia, a previously document role played by peroxisomes.

During the award period we have achieved several milestones:

1). We have identified experimental conditions for expression and purification of the stable HIPK1 kinase variants in the amounts suitable for extensive screening of crystallization conditions.

2). We have developed an in vitro enzymatic assay for measuring kinase activity of HIPK kinases and in our preliminary enzymatic studies, we have identified differences in catalytic rates between different HIPK homologs and mutants.

3). We have generated a suite of recombinant HIPK expression constructs that represent all members of the HIPK (HIPK1, HIPK2, HIPK3 and HIPK4) family that sets the stage for comparative analysis of their structures by X-ray crystallography and their activity by enzymatic studies.

4). We have identified a range of FDA-approved small molecule inhibitors that bind HIPK1 and its close homolog HIPK2 and characterized their binding properties using differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF). This analysis, together with bio-informatic and in silico structural analysis of the unique HIPK kinase domain have generated hypotheses how to design HIPK1-specific compounds. After succeeding with generating stable recombinant HIPK1, we have recently begun extensive crystallography trials with the characterized compounds.

5). We have conducted in silico analysis of HIPK kinases in relation to other protein kinases, based on the deep sequence analysis using Bayesian Partitioning with Pattern Selection (BPPS). This analysis has identified positions in the sequence of HIPK kinases which distinguish them from other protein kinases and identified a previously not appreciated hydroxylation motif. Kinase hydroxylation has been shown as an essential step in regulation of closely related kinases, DYRKs, and our future studies will focus on understanding how this potential modification might regulated HIPK signaling.

In the project, we constructed cDNA libraries of CACNG proteins containing translational stop codons in specific locations. These libraries can be used to incorporate non-canonical amino acids with advantageous properties such as fluorescence or UV-reactive crosslinking. In addition to constructing libraries for 4 of these important neuronal proteins, we screened one library for incorporation of a specific non-canonical amino acid, identifying several positions that support incorporation but also positions which are poorly incorporating. We plan to complete our screens, share these libraires in commonly used repositories and use particular positions to further interrogate structure and function relationships in this neuronal protein family.

This project aimed to determine the role of a lipid kinase, PIP5K, in making a lipid molecule that is used by another lipid kinase, PI3K, to signal cellular growth and proliferation. Aberrant production of these lipid signals is a common driver of cancers. We found that modulation of PIP5K indeed producing a linear response in PI3K signaling, with more PIP5K activity causing more PI3K signals and less reducing it. However, our efforts to demonstrate utility of an inhibitor of this enzyme, isa2011b, at an anti-cancer agent were limited since we could find no evidence that the compound impacts PIP5K activity in cultured cells.

The capacity to experience reward is essential for a healthy psychological function and well-being. Hedonic tone is the ability of an individual to feel pleasure and can impact an individual’s liking towards a reward as well as the motivation and reinforcement to obtain the reward. In this project, we sought to investigate the role of GPR162 in hedonic tone. While we know that GPR162 is a highly expressed receptor in the brain, its psychological relevance is unknown. To understand the importance of this receptor in reward, we used a behavioral paradigm to study hedonic tone in mice within their home environment using sucrose as a reward. In this study, we targeted GPR162 by reducing or increasing its protein level in the nucleus accumbens, an area of the brain that plays a key role in reward-related behaviors. This finding shed light on a molecular mechanism that regulates aspects of reward behaviors.

Work conducted by Dr. Insel’s laboratory included analyses of signaling by GPR68, one of the proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Studies were conducted using an HEK293 cell line that stably expressed GPR68. Initial studies, using commercial anti-GPR68 antibodies, confirmed that GPR68 was expressed in the stably expressing HEK293 cell line but not in the parental HEK293 cells. Experiments were then undertaken to examine coupling of GPR68 to certain heterotrimeric G proteins, in particular Gs (which activates adenylyl cyclase and thereby increases production of cyclic AMP [cAMP]) and Gq/11 (which activates phospholipase C-beta and increases cellular calcium. The studies (which included assessment of time-course, concentration-response and desensitization) showed that both cAMP and calcium were increased by low pH activation of GPR68 in the HEK293 cells that stably express GPR68 but not in control HEK293 cells. Further experiments showed that the activation of phospholipase C-beta was not required for the increase in cAMP and thus, that increase in cAMP and increase in calcium occur independently with GPR68 activation by low pH. In the Chang Lab, we have over-expressed and purified GPR68 as a GFP fusion using HEK293S and CHO cells. We have noted a higher yield of GPR68 from CHO cells and 0.5 mM Ogerin is needed to facilitate proper protein fold. The HEK293S cells tend to have aggregates while the GPR68-GFP in CHO cells tend to be more uniformly localized on the cell surface. Using this material, we used our nanobody discovery platform to select for binders. Current plans are to re-transform insect Sf9 cells to increase the yield of GPR68-GFP. We have had great success making GPCRs as such and scale of material is much easier to accommodate. From this material, we plan to retest these Nbs (Fig. 2) but also generate a new panel of Nbs to further test for inhibition in collaboration with the Insel lab.

Background: Hepatic Fibrosis is a global health problem. Fibrosis encompasses the scarring of the liver in response to chronic injury, and involves secretion and deposition of matrix proteins by fibrogenic cells. The primary fibrogenic cells in the liver are the hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), which are activated upon liver injury to produce matrix proteins, chief among them, procollagen I. Procollagen I must be folded within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and trafficked through the secretory pathway, followed by exocytosis from the cell and cleavage to collagen I. We proposed that mechanisms regulating the intracellular processing and trafficking of procollagen I could be targeted to limit fibrogenesis. The ER-localized ion channel, TMEM38B, has been implicated in collagen secretion during bone formation, but had not been studied in liver physiology or pathology. This grant aimed to understand the role and regulation of TMEM38B in HSC-mediated fibrogenesis. 

Major findings: 
TMEM38B increased in patients with cirrhosis as well as mouse mouses of liver fibrosis. 
TMEM38B expression increases in fibrogenic hepatic stellate cells, and that this expression is dependent on epigenetic regulation through the Polycomb repressor complex (PRC2).  
Reduced levels of TMEM38B inhibited collagen secretion from fibrogenic hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). 
Inhibition of the PRC2 complex is sufficient to promote collagen I secretion form HSCs. 

Conclusions: Based on our findings, we conclude that TMEM38B is critical for collagen I secretion from HSCs, and could serve as a potential anti-fibrotic target.

Research in this award focused on linking targeted protein degradation to kinase activity as a means to identify substrates of three important yet understudied kinases: the NIMA-related kinases Nek6, Nek7 and Nek9. In support of these goals, we were able to generate cell lines in which a protein sequence tag was added to each of these three kinases as a marker to degrade them upon addition of a special small molecule to the cells called auxin. We were able to validate that each of these three cell lines contained all copies of each kinase as completely tagged with this degradation sequence, and that the addition of the small molecule auxin reliably depleted the kinase from the cells in a matter of minutes. Surprisingly, and in contrast to prior published reports of genetic depletion of each of these kinases by RNA interference technology, loss of each kinase was well tolerated and resulted in little to no growth defects. In addition, subsequent analysis of the signaling pathways in these cells upon kinase degradation suggests that their loss has little to no impact on cell signaling. Thus, while we were able to accomplish our initial goal of generating these unique tools to study Nek6, Nek7 and Nek9 biology, it is unclear how relevant they are to the ongoing efforts to understand how they function.

The major outcome of this award was further funding through the American Heart Association, Transformational Project Award #969976. The award also provided preliminary data for an R01 submission that is currently under review.

This project is nearly fully completed. However, we are in the process of finalizing our publication in PeerJ in a special issue entitled “Advances in Illuminating the Druggable Genome”. It has been accepted provided minor corrections and the completion of one additional control study (in progress). We anticipate this article to be published before the end of 2023. At this time, we will enter it in NCBI in association with this grant.  Moreover, we will archive data produced during this project for long-term storage (histology slides, images, etc.)  Lastly, we will keep maintaining the transgenic mice in our barrier facility for future requests.

Three Myotonic Dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinases or MRCKs alpha, beta and gamma are selective effectors for both Rac1 and Cdc42 through a CRIB domain-mediated interaction, though most studies have focused only on Cdc42 coupling. MRCKs alpha and beta are constitutively expressed and associated with cell migration and invasion in skin, breast and ovarian cancer through the phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC). Nevertheless, MRCKs are considered ‘dark’ kinases due to the limited knowledge about their signaling functions and prospective interest as targets. Here we present data on Rac1-MRCK gamma coupling in the context of ovarian cancer. Review of gene and protein expression databases indicated that MRCK gamma expression is upregulated in ovarian cancer, motivating our further functional studies. In four of six epithelial and mesenchymal ovarian cancer cell lines, MRCK gamma mRNA expression levels were 5-10 fold above those of MRCK alpha and beta. Overexpression of Rac1 in the aggressive mesothelial-like ovarian SKOV3ip cancer cell line increased MRCK gamma protein expression 2.5-fold with no corresponding change in MRCK alpha. Increased MRCK gamma protein expression resulted in increased phosphorylation of MLC, suggesting a functional regulation of MRCK gamma activity by Rac1 GTPase. Conversely, in vivo treatment of mice with R-ketorolac (a Rac1/Cdc42 inhibitor) reduced MRCK gamma expression 2-fold in SKOV3ip xenograft tumors, demonstrating importance of this signaling axis in tumor growth. Based on the published literature and in collaboration with the Illuminating the Druggable Genome Kinase Group MRCK targeting inhibitors were identified for testing. SD-208, a known TGFBRI kinase inhibitor, was found to have a Kd of 26 nM against MRCK gamma on the DiscoverX affinity selection platform for the wild-type human kinases that inhibited >80% of control in the 456 scanMAX kinase assay panel. In ovarian cancer, spheroids are the metastatic unit that detaches from the primary tumor and metastasizes to the omentum. To test MRCK gamma function in ovarian cancer cell invasion and metastasis, SKOV3ip spheroids were used in an in vitro mesothelial clearance that mimics in vivo metastatic steps. Invasion of the mesothelial layer of cells by the spheroids requires MLC phosphorylation and actinomyosin cytoskeletal remodeling. SD-208 treatment resulted in a 2.2-fold decrease in the clearance area in both parental and Rac1 overexpressing SKOV3ip cells. The mesothelial clearance data is consistent with the effects on in vivo tumor growth and inhibition of MLC phosphorylation seen in 2D cell culture studies and support a role for MRCK gamma dependent actinomysin remodeling in ovarian cell invasion and metastasis. Taken together our results support MRCK gamma as a therapeutic target in ovarian cancer.

An estimated 10 million Americans and 250 million individuals worldwide suffer from lymphedema, and yet the only recommended therapies are compression garments and manual massage.  Thus, there is a critical need to identify new pharmacological targets that could be harnessed for the improvement of lymphatic function. Results from our proposal provided enabling tools, technologies and knowledge to catalyze further, in-depth studies on the lymphatic roles of G protein coupled receptors, which represent the largest category of pharmacological targets in medicine today. We identified critical functions for Gprc5b in lymphatic developmental and during the early postnatal period as well as high expression of Gpr116 in certain adult cardiovascular tissues. Collectively, we have successfully expanded the current repertoire of GPCRs with known expression and function in lymphatic vessels.

Our data support the conclusion that GluD1 and GluD2 receptors signal by very different means.  This is demonstrated by different patterns of intolerance, different actions of variants in potential gating regions, and different effects of variants in the agonist binding domain.  In addition, we identified intolerant portions of the distal end of the receptor that binds Cbln family of proteins, confirming this is a function of the receptors that is essential for normal brain function.  We also show that key gating regions in GRID1 are less sensitive to variation than GRID2, suggesting that GluD1 is unlikely to function as an ion channel. However, as a caveat, we confirm a recent report that tethering of two amino terminal domains together with Cbln proteins can produce an inward current, so there may be contexts in which GluD1 can pass agonist-evoked currents.

Outcomes

Regulated cell migration is critical for the repair of tissue damage and is hijacked during the metastasis of cancer cells.  Cell movement requires that attachments anchoring cells to their environment be released at the rear of the cell and that new attachments are formed as the cells move forward.  The proteins that anchor cells are continuously internalized from the cell surface, moved to the front of the cell, and then externalized back to the surface to form the new attachments.  We have evidence suggesting that the transient production of a key membrane lipid at compartments within cells is essential for delivering these proteins back to the surface of migrating cells.  Several different enzymes can make this lipid.  The goal of this project is to identify which of these enzymes produce the lipid during recycling of attachment proteins to the cell surface.  We have found that 2 of them, PIP5K1A and PIP5K1C, are essential for this process.  We have also determined that the attachment proteins are getting trapped during the later steps in cell surface delivery when the lipid is not made.

We have generated constructs of GPR32 that showed high expression levels of GPR32 in Sf9 cells. However, after many times of experiments during the period of this grant, we failed to produce functional GPR32 protein using the putative ligand RvD1 that is suitable for structural studies. Our current effort on GPR32 is to obtain the ligand-free apo-receptor in complex with Gi. We have directed our effort to another orphan GPCR, GPR171, and generated promising preliminary results toward the structural elucidation of GPR171. We have tested our approach of structure-based development of GPCR ligands on FPR1 and successfully obtained a new antagonist. We will take a similar approach to develop novel GPR32 ligands using the modeled structure or the structure of the apo-GPR32-Gi complex we will obtain in the future.

Epilepsy is a condition affecting millions of people worldwide, with a vast majority of those people living in low- and middle-income countries. Unfortunately, the molecular mechanisms involved in epilepsy syndromes are poorly understood. This proposal aimed to investigate a protein termed MAST3, which is newly implicated in the development of childhood epilepsy. The results supported our central hypothesis, namely that disease-relevant mutations in MAST3 caused a gain-of-function phenotype resulting from aberrant changes in the phosphorylation of MAST3 substrate(s). Since MAST3 is expressed in common brain areas for epileptic seizures, such as the hippocampus, cerebral cortex, and striatum, and new genetic research has identified mutations in MAST3 associated with epilepsy, investigating the signaling partners and function of MAST3 can potentially lead to the development of novel therapies for childhood developmental neurological disorders.

Given the limited treatments for chronic pain especially for females, we set out to evaluate GPR171 as a novel target in both sexes. Previously we showed that activating GPR171 led to enhanced morphine induced analgesia in male mice. In these current studies we investigated the effectiveness of GPR171 agonist on acute and chronic pain. In addition to side effects after repeated injections. These are the main findings of our studies:
1. GPR171 agonist releives increased pain senstivites after neuropathic pain in males only
2. Neuropathic pain causes a reduction in GPR171 in key brain areas involved in pain
3. GPR171 agonist enhances morphine analgesia in females like we previously found in males
4. GPR171 agonist does not enahnce morphine tolerance, withdrawal, or reward in either sex
5. GPR171 agonist does not produce reward or activate rewarding areas of the brain

Our project set out a goal to improve our understanding of specific potassium channels that are understudied but etiological determinants of multiple pathological conditions including, but not limited to, type II diabetes, inflammation, arthritis, and proximal renal tubular acidosis. To achieve the goal, we have successfully established experimental setups to express and purify the proteins at the levels, with which we can do functional assays and structure determinations via electron microscopy. Also, we have established a protocol to discover nanobodies (small antibodies from a camel) specific to the protein of interest in the lab. Unfortunately, our target proteins are highly unstable when they are isolated and therefore most of our experiments failed to support solid conclusions. Yet we have discovered that one of our target proteins makes a very strong interaction with a small soluble protein, and there is a high chance that the interaction of the small protein has a functional implication, which is under investigation currently and may lead to a discovery of novel regulatory mechanism of the protein in cells.

Chloride channels and their regulators are recognized as keys to control ion regulation and excitability in essentially all cells, which has made them important therapeutic targets. The calcium-activated chloride channel regulator (CLCA) family of proteins (CLCA1, 2, 4) have been associated with and suggested as drug targets for a number of diseases including asthma, COPD, cystic fibrosis (CF), Crohn’s disease, infectious diarrhea, ulcerative colitis, and some cancers. However, a detailed understanding of their biological functions has lagged far behind their association with these diseases. In this pilot project, we focused on the vastly understudied calcium-activated chloride channel  regulator CLCA4, which we believe plays a much more important biological role than can be currently assessed due to the lack of basic biochemical knowledge and tools. We have completed work showing that CLCA4 specifically potentiates the calcium-activated chloride channel TMEM16B. In addition, our work shows that CLCA4 uses a mechanism similar to CLCA1. In other words, CLCA4 contains a matrix-metalloprotease-like domain that is required cleave CLCA4 into two pieces (N-CLCA4 and C-CLCA4), and then N-CLCA4 binds to and potentiates TMEM16B. The interaction is mediated by a metal-ion-dependent adhesion site (MIDAS) in the CLCA4 VWA domain. The results suggest distinct functional interactions between CLCA and TMEM16 family members that may be relevant to multiple diseases.

Dual specificity protein kinases perform indispensable roles in eukaryotes including the regulation of signal transduction pathways and subcellular compartmentalization. Structurally, in addition to their folded kinase domains, they are composed of significantly long segments that are intrinsically disordered. These intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) feature multivalent low-complexity sequences. Whereas the folded domains of these kinases are studied extensively (both biochemically and structurally), little is known about the functional role of the disordered low-complexity domains (LCDs) that display a compositional bias towards polar and charged amino acids. Before this grant award, we and others have established that multivalent LCDs can undergo dynamic self-assembly into liquid droplets through intracellular phase separation. However, one key unanswered question is how LCD primary sequences encode selective homotypic interactions driving their self-assembly into liquid-like droplets. 
In this project, we characterized the molecular code of intracellular phase-separation of the arginine and serine-rich LCD (285 amino acids long) of dual specificity kinase CLK3. We systematically generated several engineered fluorescently-tagged variants of CLK3 LCD for mammalian cell expression and visualization to study the localization and phase separation of this LCD in the cell nucleus. Our main findings are as follows:

•	We confirmed that CLK3 LCD is important for nuclear localization of CLK3. This is LCD also needed for the protein’s localization into nuclear speckles

•	To test the intracellular phase separation capacity, we created an optogenetic version of CLK3 LCD (optoCLK3-LCD). Using live cell imaging, we observed that optoCLK3-LCD can form intracellular condensates under blue light activation implying that the LCD has an intrinsic ability to undergo phase separation in the nucleus.

•	We characterized the role of arginine residues in CLK3 LCD phase separation and nuclear speckle localization by creating a series of Arg-to-Lys mutants. This approach may help us to better understand the critical roles of arginine residues in CLK3 LCD function, not achievable by Lys residues although it carries the same charge as Arg.

•	We found that phospho-mimicking variants of CLK3 LCD display improved phase separation capacity in live cells, suggesting a key role of Ser phosphorylation in CLK3’s phase separation and nuclear speckle formation/localization.

•	We discovered that CLK3 LCD forms coexisting condensates with the prion-like domain (PLD) of RNA-binding protein FUS in the cell nucleus, indicating that there exist selective LCD sequence codes across functionally distinct nuclear proteins that govern discrete co-condensate formation in the cell nucleus.

The purpose of this proposal was to generate new reagents for studying and manipulating the function of alpha2delta proteins encoded by CACNA2D2 and CACNA2D3 genes. These proteins are most well known as auxiliary subunits of high-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels but may have other functions as well and are potentially promising drug targets. We have generated reagents enabling the expression and purification of alpha2delta subunits, their detection on the surface of cells using fluorescent toxins as probes, and isolated potential nanobody binders that are currently being characterized and validated. These new tools will advance the study of these proteins and their utility as potential drug targets.

Cdkl1 kinase is an understudied protein. Our work has provided the first insights into the functional relevance of this kinase. We show that Cdkl1 is not required for normal mice development, however, it plays a detrimental role during the development of acute kidney injury. These results suggest that Cdkl1 is a druggable target for acute kidney injury, a common disease that currently has no treatments and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality.

Zebrafish are vertebrate model organisms that are becoming popular for the functional analysis of genes. We planned to use zebrafish and CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technology to create mutations in 28 understudied protein kinase genes. We identified these genes based on their potential roles in developmental disorders. This project generated important preliminary data by examining the functional impact of these 28 understudied protein kinases in zebrafish. Our data show that 16 out of 28 genes exhibit early developmental phenotypes. These models can be used to understand the pathophysiology of human diseases and for further drug screening. We will also share these fish lines and associated phenotype information with the scientific community through a publication, as well as through a public database, Zebrafish Information Network (ZFIN).

Many of the drugs in the modern pharmacopeia target G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) or kinases, yet a large number of these proteins have yet to be targeted successfully for therapeutic purposes. The goal of our one-year R03 project was to test a new hypothesis that many such “dark” GPCRs and kinases communicate directly with one another. Successful completion of our project will increase our understanding of how GPCRs and kinases function within cells and provide new concepts and tools to identify drugs that target these proteins. We also expect our findings to have implications for cancer, metabolic disorders, and a range of other human diseases.

During the period of this award, we made substantial progress developing a high-throughput screening platform known as PRESTO-TANGO to systematically identify interactions between GPCRs and the catalytic subunit of PKA (PKA-C), a pleiotropic, multifunctional kinase involved in myriad biological processes. We performed extensive testing and optimization, benchmarking our assay using SMOOTHENED, a GPCR we previously identified to directly bind to PKA-C. Through these efforts, we found that the PRESTO-TANGO system is well-suited to identify direct GPCR / PKA-C interactions. Specifically, PRESTO-TANGO readily detected specific SMOOTHENED / PKA-C interactions along with several novel GPCR / PKA-C interactions, all in a convenient, sensitive, and straightforward manner. Furthermore, the data from our PRESTO-TANGO assay displayed excellent signal-to-noise comparable to that obtained from the more conventional, low-throughput assays we utilized in our previous work on SMOOTHENED. With this valuable information in hand, we are now poised to begin systematically screening the entire collection of human GPCRs for direct interactions with PKA-C in the very near future.

To understand which IDG kinases are expressed in T cells, we performed unbiased analyses of published datasets. These revealed DYRK1B and DYRK2 as the IDG kinases that are most highly expressed in T cells. We used CRISPR-editing experiments in human T cells to understand which of these is involved in Treg differentiation. We found that editing of DYRK1B, but not of DYRK2, enhanced Treg differentiation. These results identify DYRK1B as a novel regulator of Treg differentiation. Of note, the magnitude of the pro-Treg effect secondary to DYRK1B editing was significantly less than that observed with harmine treatment. Whether this reflects incomplete loss of DYRK1B during CRISPR-editing versus other target of harmine remains to be clarified.

By focusing on a poorly understood kinase, DYRK2, we helped to elucidate molecular mechanisms central to Hedgehog signal transduction, a way in which cells communicate, with implications for skeletal development and cancer formation. Elucidating how DYRK2 functions in ciliary Hedgehog signaling helps reveal not only mechanisms of signal transduction, but also how human diseases caused by ciliary defects, ciliopathies, cause birth defects and how misactivated Hedgehog signaling causes cancers such as medulloblastoma, the most common brain cancer among children.

The goals of this project were to test whether four novel protein kinase genes are involved in regulating sleep by performing gain- and loss-of-function studies in zebrafish, and to begin to determine how these genes regulate sleep using phosphoproteomic studies. We succeeded in showing that loss-of-function mutations in three of the four genes results in robust sleep phenotypes in zebrafish. Phosphoproteomic analyses for one of these genes revealed potential mechanisms through which this protein kinase may affect sleep, which we will explore in future studies.

Ion channels are membrane proteins that underlie all of the electrical signaling in our body, including the brain and the heart. Given this role, they are extremely important for health and human disease and are frequently the target of drugs. Despite their well-documented importance, little is known about some ion channels, including the understudied channels KCNH4 and KCNH8.  Our goal was to determine the potential of these channels as a target for future drugs by first studying how the channels work.  One major barrier for studying how a channel, or any protein, works is measuring their structural dynamics, the submicroscopic movements of these proteins that underlie their function.  In this granting period, we have developed a method using fluorescent probes to measure these movements and applied this method to a model ion channel. These studies lay the groundwork for the design of better drugs that target KCNH4 and KCNH8 or, indeed, any of the understudied proteins that might be useful drug targets.

In this study, we identified that members of the ROCK2 family of kinases control myofibroblast-mediated fibrosis. Protein-protein interaction studies with Cdc42bpg, one of the ROCK family members,  demonstrate that the Hippo signaling cascade is an upstream regulatory component. This further reveals that mechanical forces will modulate the strength of signaling by Cdc42bpg Functional redundancy between members of this kinase family indicates that several members would need to be targeted by pharmacotherapy to effectively mitigate fibrosis.

FAM26F is an understudied ion channel that belongs to a small family of proteins (FAM26A to FAM26F). It is highly expressed in a specific subset of immune cells called macrophages that promote inflammation in different disease contexts, including rheumatoid arthritis, a common autoimmune disease affecting about 1.3 million patients in the US. The molecular function of FAM26F is unknown but may involve ion channel activity. In this exploratory project, we analyzed the putative ion channel function of FAM26F under different experimental conditions but were unable to corroborate that FAM26F carries ion currents or transports small biomolecules across the cell membrane, at least under the conditions tested. A second goal of this project was to explore the effects of FAM26F on the function of macrophages. Using genetic deletion of FAM26F in cultured macrophages, we observed reduced levels of cytokines and other proinflammatory molecules, demonstrating that FAM26F is required for proinflammatory macrophage functions. We successfully generated genetically engineered mice that lack FAM26F and its homologue FAM26E to study the role of both putative ion channels in rheumatoid arthritis.

This study helped to define the function of VRK2, a gene that is associated with multiple neuropsychiatric disorders and also sleep. The overarching goal is to determine the targets of Vrk2 in the developing brain. We use larval zebrafish for these studies, and we had previously published an initial characterization of a zebrafish line lacking vrk2, which had changes to behavior and brain activity.

To accomplish our goal, we optimized a method for finding proteins that interact with Vrk2 for use in the developing zebrafish larvae. The proteomics results from these tissue samples revealed both targets expected from the literature, from studies of cell lines such as cancers, and ones more specific to brain development. In addition, we determined what pathways were dysregulated at later ages of development, when the previously identified neural phenotypes were observed. These pathways, found with mRNA sequencing, matched published literature from cell lines, similar to the proteomics data. The disrupted pathways included DNA damage, chromatin, and cell cycle. However, the experiment also revealed novel changes to genes that specifically mark the habenula region of the brain. This finding lines up with proteomics, as one interacting partner had previously been found to have a role in habenula development. The habenula has known roles in light responsivity, which could be involved in sleep regulation, as well as multiple neuropsychiatric disorders.

In addition, we developed a new tool for future studies of Vrk2 – a version of the protein that can accept a non-natural substrate or analog that allows for the direct addition of an orthogonal tag to Vrk2 targets. We confirmed that this Vrk2 variant was functional both in enzyme assays and in the context of a developing zebrafish.

During the one year of the RO3 funding  we made significant strides in elucidating the roles of the CACNA2D2 and CACNA2D3 proteins in regulating synaptic function. We demonstrated that CACNA2D2 and CACNA2D3 mRNA is highly expressed in the cochlear nucleus while CACNA2D1 mRNA is undetectable. We generated novel CACNA2D transgenic mouse lines. We found that complete loss of CACNA2D1, CACNA2D2, and CACNA2D3 at the calyx of Held/MNTB synapse are not key proteins that regulate synapse morphology or active zone ultrastructure, but they are essential regulators presynaptic voltage-gated CaV2 calcium channels.  We a demonstrated that they are not key determinants of the organization of presynaptic voltage-gated CaV2 calcium channels. Using our novel CACNA2D transgenic mouse lines to individually CACNA2D2 or CACNA2D3  we demonstrated that CACNA2D2 and CACNA2D3 have distinct roles in regulating synaptic transmission and plasticity. All in all, we have developed new insights and paradigms that will serve  as a foundation in our overall goal in elucidating the roles of the CACNA2D proteins in regulating synaptic function and neuronal circuit output.

Testis-specific serine kinases (TSSKs) belong to AMPK-related kinase family. Loss-of-function mutants of some TSSK members lead to spermatogenesis defects in male mice, and several SNPs of TSSKs are associated with male infertility in humans.  However, the TSSK signaling mechanism during spermatogenesis is not understood. This proposal employs Drosophila as a model system to investigate a novel kinase-substrate pair: TSSKs-class IIa HDACs. These are the major findings.

•	HDAC4 is a TSSK substrate in test-tube and in cell.
•	TSSK-mediated phosphorylation of HDAC4 leads to its nucleus-to-cytosol translocation.
•	Modulation of TSSK-HDAC4 pathway affects male fertility in Drosophila.

In this project, we tested the regulation of the orphan G protein coupled receptor Gprc5b by retinoic acid in mice. We confirmed that chronic treatments with retinoic acid induced depressive-like behaviors in mice, and we found that Gprc5b expression levels were selectively increased in a subpopulation of neurons within the hippocampus. These cells are neuronal progenitors that play a fundamental role in the development and progression of depression in patients and depressive-like behaviors in rodents. We further generated a global Gprc5b knockout (KO) mouse model to explore the role of this important orphan receptor in establishing depressive-like behaviors. Gprc5b KO mice have been phenotyped with a battery of behavioral tests and the results suggest they could be resilient to retinoic acid-induced changes in mouse behavior. Further work will clarify if Gprc5b is a key mediator of the behavioral effects of retinoic acid.

This project was part of the Illuminating the Druggable Genome initiative, which aims to better understand poorly studied proteins belonging to families that have been successful targets for drug development. Protein kinases in particular include targets of nearly 100 FDA approved drugs. Our research focused on two protein kinases called ERK4 and ERK7. Protein kinases toggle between active and inactive forms, and when active they act as enzymes that phosphorylate other proteins. In this research project, we established techniques that allow us to identify human protein fragments, or peptides, that bind to each kinase. Using these techniques, we identified dozens of peptides that interact specifically with either ERK4 or ERK7. The proteins corresponding to these peptides may control activity of these kinases or alternatively may act as their substrates.

Asthma is a common chronic disease and a major public health concern. Standard treatments—β2-adrenergic receptor agonists, corticosteroids, and monoclonal antibodies—manage symptoms and exacerbations but raise concerns about long-term safety and efficacy, and they do not address airway remodeling, a hallmark of severe disease. Bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs), a subset of GPCRs expressed beyond the oral cavity, including airway smooth muscle (ASM), have emerged as attractive therapeutic targets. Agonists such as quinine promote bronchodilation, suppress inflammation, regulate ASM proliferation, and improve remodeling in animal models. These findings highlight TAS2Rs as promising candidates for asthma therapy and have generated strong mechanistic and translational interest. Despite these advances, the mechanistic basis of TAS2R-mediated therapeutic effects remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we initiated this pilot R03 project by generating multiple Tas2r-deficient mouse lines using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing. We performed extensive genotyping using various strategies, including PCR/sequencing, and created compound mutants through breeding strategies. We further assessed mutant responses to bitter agonists using two-bottle preference tests, and ongoing phenotyping includes flexiVent-based pulmonary function analysis.

Chloride Intracellular Ion Channels (CLICs) are the unique class of proteins which exist in soluble and membranous form. They are listed under understudied proteins. We took over the newest family member of CLICs, CLIC6 which has a longer N-terminus, and their basic biophysical properties were not established. We completed the project with publishing electrophysiological properties and regulation mechanism of these unique ion channels. We have identified amino acids responsible for regulation of CLIC6 by pH. In addition, we also determine that CLIC6 is redox regulated ion channels and Cys residue at the top of the trans membrane domain is the key redox sensor. 
Key findings for the proposal are
1.	CLIC6 forms an ion channel in the plasma membrane of HEK 293 cells
2.	CLIC6 localizes to plasma membrane and mitochondrial membranes of MLE cells.
3.	We also discovered CLIC4 is associated with mitochondrial membranes.
4.	Our group has also shown that intracellular ion channels can affect the heart function of flies.
5.	We have successfully established the clic6 null mutant mouse colony for future proposals.
6.	We determined Cl levels and how it is involved in cellular homeostasis.

The work related to this project established the localization of ADGRA3 within the liver.  We subsequently determined that this receptor is also highly expressed within the kidney and used the existing resources that were acquired from this funding to localize the receptor to the distal tubule and connecting tubule.  While the studies were initiated in mice, we were able to obtain human liver and kidney sections and confirmed that ADGRA3 is also highly expressed in human liver and kidney.  We also established that this receptor, an atypical adhesion GPCR, does undergo cleavage and can self-activate via a tethered agonist.  We confirmed that it exhibits a high degree of constitutive activity and can also be activated by several other exogenous compounds.  Initial studies have indicated that there is a defect in bile production in the Adgra3 knockout mouse.  As these mice were obtained late in the funding cycle, we are in the process of conducting additional phenotyping experiments to fully elucidate the role of ADGRA3 within the adult liver and kidney. 

A manuscript reporting our initial findings is in preparation.  In addition, our work on ADGRA3 in the kidney resulted in the application of a grant to the American Society for Nephrology.  Finally, another grant is in progress and will be submitted to the NIH in February 2025.

AMPA type ionotropic glutamate receptors (AMPARs) are ligand gated ion channels that mediate the majority of excitatory synaptic transmission in our brain. The function of calcium permeable AMPARs (CP-AMPARs) is highly relevant to ischemic brain damages, brain tumors, addiction, fear-conditioning, and motor function. Compounds that selectively target type-II TARP containing CP-AMPARs are promising reagents for pharmacological manipulation to study the cellular function of these complexes and may facilitate the future development of drugs for treating the pathological conditions. Our goal is to establish the structural basis for the mechanism of type-II TARP function, by solving high-resolution structures of a type-II TARP in complex with CP-AMPAR GluA1. As of the end of the funding period we continue to make efforts into solving the cryo-EM structure. At the moment, the key outcome of this research is the generation of tandemized GluA1-TARPgamma5 and GluA1-TARPgamma7 constructs that form functional ion channels when expressed in HEK cells. The stable cell lines that express these constructs in DOX dependent fashion will be available in due course. These constructs were functionally validated by electrophysiology recordings, and thus could be used directly for high throughput drug screening using calcium flux assay.

Potassium channels help regulate electrical signals in the brain and nervous system. In this project, we studied a specific group of these channels called KvS subunits, which are not well understood but play important roles in controlling how neurons work. Our goal was to develop new tools to study these proteins and learn more about where they are found and what they do in the nervous system.
Main Findings:
•	New Antibody for Kv6.4: We developed a specialized antibody that can detect the Kv6.4 protein in spinal cord tissue. This antibody is now available for use by other researchers to help study Kv6.4 and its role in the nervous system.
•	Genetically Modified Kv6.4: We created a version of Kv6.4 that can be tagged with fluorescent markers. This allowed us to see where it is located in cells and also made it possible to control its activity using a chemical compound. This approach could help us understand how Kv6.4 is involved in pain and migraine.
•	Location of Kv6.4 in Neurons: We found that Kv6.4 is present in motor neurons in the spinal cord. We also discovered that KvS subunits are important in sensory neurons that are involved in feeling pain. This makes them potential targets for treating pain.

Polycystins, a unique class of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels with unknown regulation - Two groups of polycystins exist in mammals and are classified as having either 11-transmembrane (TM) or 6-TM helices; PKD1 and its homologues PKD1-L1, PKD1-L2 and PKD1-L3 fall into the 11-TM class, while PKD2 and its homologues PKD2-L1 and PKD2-L2 (also called polycystin2’s, PC2’s or TRPPs) fall into the 6-TM class (Fig 1). The 11-TM polycystins alone are likely unable to form a functional channel. Instead, 11-TM PKD1 members associate with 6-TM polycystins (PKD2) to form heteromeric complexes. Recently published cryo-EM structures demonstrated that PKD2 can form a homomeric or heteromeric channel complex. Strikingly, the recently reported cryo-EM structure of a partial PKD1/PKD2 heteromer revealed a rather unusual 3 PKD2 : 1 PKD1 subunit assembly3, as has also been suggested based on biochemical evidence1. 
Association of an 11-TM protein with a pore forming 6-TM TRP ion channel is unique among the TRP superfamily and how PKD1 family members contribute functionally to the core channel complex remains an unanswered fundamental question. The PKD1 family is also unique as a channel subunit in that members contain a large N-terminal extracellular region decorated with a multitude of putative adhesive and/or ligand-binding domains. Further, the entire PKD1 N-terminus can be cleaved via a GPS autoproteolytic site and may function as a secreted ligand. Thus combining PKD1 members with PKD2 channels into a signaling complex has the potential to transmit adhesion and other as-yet unidentified ligand interactions to ion permeation.

We are extremely grateful for the generous support from the IDG consortium. In the past one-year funding period, we were able to generate significant preliminary data (e.g., new PKD2L2 cryo-EM structure) which we included in a recent R01 application. We will continue to demystify PKD2L2 using structural and biochemical/biophysical approaches based on the foundational studies enabled by the R03 pilot grant. We expect that our PKD2L2 research will be supported by other funding mechanisms. This R03 grant also supported the training of the graduate student Sreeja Govindarajan who have learned molecular biology and membrane protein biochemistry and structural biology. Finally, we expect to obtain PKD2L2-binding nanobodies in the near future. We will share these nanobodies with IDG and distribute them to the broad academic community once we have done in-depth characterization.

Key outcome:
1.	GPR68 activation repressed inflammatory gene expression in primary human chondrocytes stimulated with IL1β at low pH (6.4).
2.	Loss of GPR68 in human chondrocytes exacerbated matrix degrading protease expression including MMP13, MMP3 and ADAMTs4.
3.	GPR68 act as acid sensing receptor in human chondrocytes and sense low pH during OA progression and stimulate downstream signaling to counteract effect of acidosis in chondrocytes.
4.	Gpr68 knockout mice upon DMM surgery induced accelerated progression of PTOA and showed enhanced cartilage erosion, increased subchondral bone sclerosis, and increased osteophyte formation.
5.	Gpr68 knockout mice showed augmented synovial inflammation as indicated by enhanced synovial thickening, more synovitis and increased immune cell infiltration.

Using this pilot funding from the IDG, we successfully generated human pluripotent stem cells with a single basepair mutation in an ER chloride channel that was identified in human patients. We also were able to show, using single cell RNA sequencing, what the transcriptional outcomes of loss of this gene are in stem cell derived islets. Finally, we were able to eventually obtain a line of mice that harbor this same mutation. These data further our understanding of this channel and will be valuable preliminary data for a future R01 application on this topic.

Adhesion G protein-coupled receptors (aGPCRs) are a group of 33 poorly characterized non-olfactory GPCRs with distinct features including autocatalytic processing and large extracellular regions. aGPCRs are involved in a myriad of biological processes and some of them are associated with diseases, especially a wide range of cancers. The extracellular regions of many of the aGPCRs contain domains that are known to be involved in protein-protein interactions, suggesting that binding to cell surface protein ligands may play an important role in their mechanism of action. The majority of aGPCRs, however, are orphan receptors without known binding partners, or ligands. Identification of ligands for these aGPCRs should help understand their physiological functions and roles in cancer development. A major challenge for identifying ligands involved in ligand-receptor interactions at the cell-cell interface is that they tend to bind their receptors very weakly and currently available methods do not have enough sensitivity. In this study, we explored a novel screening technology to overcome this hurdle. This highly sensitive and cell-based approach was used to screen a collection of transmembrane proteins to identify ligand candidates for the aGPCRs. The feasibility of the approach has been tested using model ligands and receptors that are known bind to each other with low affinities. Specifically, we generated molecular and cellular tools for four orphan aGPCRs to be used with the new technology. We also identify a potential ligand for one of the orphan aGPCRs. Their interaction and roles in physiological function will be further characterized in future studies. Finally, we have learned how to optimize certain aspects of the technology for future applications.

Outcomes of this research

The significant stories that were developed here include a first story on the control of feeding preference by GPR75, a G-protein coupled receptor that appears to be one of the most powerful mutations causing reduced weight gain in human populations.  We find this gene, when knockout out in mice, does cause a reduction in weight gain, driven by reduced feeding.  In particular, the reduced feeding appears to reflect a reduced preference for fatty foods.  This result supports that a synthetic GPR75 agonist could cause reduction in feeding control, a potential major contribution to the current campaign against obesity.  
Another major outcome was the discovery that another major receptor, GPR135, is ciliary and linked to an obesity phenotype.  The importance of this result will be further established in new studies.  We also explained another major mutation causing alterations to weight gain and metabolism.  
Finally, we found a third receptor GPR63 can elicit signaling, potentially through the known cAMP signaling pathway, and a specific effect that dramatically elongates primary cilia when overexpressed.  We believe that GPR63 may play a strong role in obesity control and thus this ability of GPR63 to change dramatically during its signaling could be a key marker for the activation of this receptor in metabolic disease.  Further studies will identify the ligand for this marker and potential chemical matter.

Together, these results further support the view that a number of specific GPCRs control obesity via ciliary pathways.  Accordingly, the large number of ciliary mutations we observe in rare Mendelian disease and in critical variants identified in GWAS studies support further efforts to explain how ciliary lesions define obesity susceptibiltiy.

Project: "Defining the MAST4 interactome in brain development and epilepsy"
Contact PI: Kimberly A. Aldinger, PhD
Organization: Seattle Children's Research Institute

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are severe childhood epilepsies that require rapid diagnosis to initiate treatment that will control seizures and prevent or reverse the loss of neurologic function. We identified de novo variants in the MAST4 gene in patients with developmental delay, DEE, vision abnormalities, and in some, structural brain abnormalities. MAST4 is a member of an understudied family of serine threonine kinases (MAST1-4 and MAST-like) that is among the IDG-eligible proteins with high potential to impact human health as a therapeutic target for epilepsy. However, no investigation into the consequences of MAST4 mutations or MAST4 in brain development has been performed. To address this gap in knowledge, we characterized MAST4 expression in multiple cell types and assessed the cellular localization of mutant MAST4. 

These were some of our main findings:
- We show that MAST4 protein localizes to microtubules in multiple cell types
- We show that wildtype and mutant MAST4 localizes to the cytoplasm of cells

Genetic interrogations in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that cyclin dependent kinase 19 (CDK19) controls vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC) dedifferentiation into synthetic SMCs thereby contributing to neointimal hyperplasia in injured arteries. 

In cultured vascular SMCs, we uncovered that CDK19 and its paralog CDK8 redundantly and additively promote vascular SMC dedifferentiation into synthetic SMCs. In a mouse model of occlusive vascular remodeling in carotid arteries induced complete ligation, we found that CDK19 promotes vascular remodeling towards vascular occlusion with minimal impact on neointima formation in injured arteries. 

These results indicate a unique role of CDK19 in occlusive vascular remodeling and lesion formation, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting CDK19 in suppressing occlusive vascular lesion formation.

In this project, we created endothelial-specific MLK2 knockout mice to study the role of MLK2 in endothelial function and tumor angiogenesis. Our findings suggest that MLK2 plays a role in endothelial cell migration and the development of subcutaneous LLC1 tumors.

Ion channels and transporters facilitate the movement of charged ions across lipid membranes. They play important roles in the function of neurons, muscle, kidney and many other cell types and organs. There are hundreds of channels and transporters, and a majority of them are relatively well characterized. There are, however, many others that are understudied, including members of the tweety family (TTYH1, TTYH2, and TTYH3) of ion channels. TTYH2 was initially characterized as a volume-regulated anion channel that predominantly transports chloride in response to cell swelling. More recent structural analyses, however, could not identify structural features that are consistent with known characteristics of an anion channel pore. We hypothesized that TTYH2 might either be a regulatory subunit of the volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) or that it may have non-channel functions. We had proposed to investigate whether TTYH2 proteins act as components of anion channels by studying cells in which TTYH2 has been deleted (Aim 1). Following an alternative hypothesis based on preliminary data that suggested that TTYH2 functions as a regulator of immune responses, we analyzed the effects of TTYH2 deletion on the function of macrophages (Aim 2), which are essential for many aspects of immunity to infection or tumors and in inflammation. 

Some of the key findings of our study are: 
- TTYH2 is expressed in bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) from mice. Expression levels decrease when BMDM are polarized towards proinflammatory M1 macrophages and increase in alternatively activated M2 macrophages. 
- When TTYH2 is overexpressed in a human macrophage cell line it localizes to the plasma membrane. 
- Volume regulated anion channels (VRAC) are present in bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) from mice and their currents display current-voltage relationships typical of VRAC channels.
- Deletion of TTYH2 in BMDM does not reduce VRAC currents, which suggests that TTYH2 is not an essential component of the VRAC complex in macrophages. 
- TTYH2 suppresses the ability of macrophages to produce inflammatory cytokines that play important roles in immunity to infection and tumors. 
- TTYH2 regulates several signaling pathways in macrophages and thereby controls macrophage function.

Project: “Analysis of KCNK12 in Dopaminergic Neuroprotection”
Contact PI: Kim A. Caldwell, PhD
Organization: The University of Alabama

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder characterized by the loss of specific brain cells that produce dopamine. A major culprit in this disease is a protein called alpha-synuclein, which builds up in these cells and causes toxicity. Another hallmark of the disease is damage to mitochondria, which act as the essential energy factories for our cells.
