Our research focused on understanding exactly how this toxic protein damages these energy factories and, more importantly, how we can intervene to protect dopamine-producing brain cells called neurons.

In this project, we modeled the neuron damage using microscopic roundworms (Caenorhabditis elegans), as a living, intact model system. We completed a series of experiments to map the destruction and identified new ways to block it. Our completed research yielded the following scientific results:
•	Through genetic screening, we identified a highly protective protein channel known as TWK-14 in roundworms and KCNK12 in humans.
•	We determined that the KCNK12/TWK-14 channel works within the brain’s circuitry as a synaptic feedback loop to maintain dopamine balance and inherently protect dopamine-producing cells from dying.
•	We performed a large-scale genetic screen and uncovered two new compensatory genetic pathways that can step in to protect neurons when normal cellular stress responses fail. 

This project successfully illuminated a hidden mechanism of how brain cells die in Parkinson’s disease. By discovering that understudied proteins like KCNK12 can serve as natural protectors of dopamine cells, we have laid a physiologically relevant foundation for new therapeutic drug discovery. Ultimately these findings could guide future treatments for Parkinson’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders caused by cellular energy failure and abnormal brain signaling.

1.	Candidate DYRK inhibitor compounds have been identified for structure-activity analysis and testing in vivo.
2.	In vitro screening has been refined and improved for testing of additional DYRK inhibitor compounds.
3.	Confocal immunohistochemical analysis is being refined to analyze murine prostate tissues after short-term animal testing of selected compounds.

This research project aimed to understand the role of TTYH1, an understudied protein, in brain cell function—particularly how it helps cells break down and recycle lipids called sphingolipids. Using computer modeling and lab experiments, we discovered that TTYH1 specifically interacts with certain types of sphingolipids, but not with other lipids such as free fatty acids. In brain cells called glial cells from both flies and mammals, TTYH1 helps process and remove these lipids through an organelle called endolysosome, which is critical to degradation and recycling of biomolecules. When TTYH1 is missing, the buildup of certain lipids, especially a signaling lipid called ceramide 1-phosphate (C1P), disrupts this cleanup process and causes problems for the cell. We also pinpointed two specific amino acids of the TTYH1 protein that are essential for its ability to handle these lipids. Without these key amino acid residues, cells become less efficient at removing lipids from endolysosomes. 

These findings are especially important because problems with lipid metabolism and autophagy are linked to aging and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s. By uncovering how TTYH1 regulates these processes, this work improves our fundamental understanding of cellular mechanisms in health and disease.

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common form of cardiac arrhythmia affecting up to 2% of population with estimated individual lifetime risk of 25%-30%. The frontline therapies such as beta blockers and Ca2+ channels blockers help control cardiac rate but do not prevent AF. The discovery of atria-specific targets to treat AF is urgent task of great importance. Recently, small conductance Ca2+ activated K+ (SK) channels have emerged as a plausible atria-specific anti-arrhythmic target, given their limited functional roles in ventricular cardiomyocytes from healthy hearts. 
SK channels gating is controlled exclusively by Ca2+ that gives them unique capacity to translate intracellular Ca2+ signals into sarcolemma repolarization. Furthermore, SK channels were found in inner mitochondrial membrane as well (mSKs). mSK activation can reduce disease-associated mito-Ca2+ overload and/ or excessive production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) that can damage numerous intracellular systems and signaling pathways and affect function of Ca2+ transport machinery members. Therefore, SK channels may play significant roles in atrial arrhythmias by affecting both Ca2+-dependent arrhythmia trigger and reentry. 
The objective of our study was to establish the roles of SK channels, and SK1 subtype in particular, in atrial cardiomyocytes from normal hearts and hearts with atrial fibrillation. 
Using mouse model of Ca2+-dependent atrial fibrillation and human induced pluripotent stem cells-derived atrial-like cardiomyocytes we found that SK channels enhancement significantly reduce pro-arrhythmic disturbances in intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis and Ca2+-dependent instabilities in electrical signals in atrial cells. We found that enhancing SK channels activity not only mitigate depolarizing force of spontaneous Ca2+ release mediated by hyperactive sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) residing Ca2+ channels ryanodine receptors (RyR2s, but also reduces their activity. We found abnormally high rate of production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by mitochondria that leads to oxidation of RyR2s from diseased hearts making them hyperactive. Enhancement of mitochondrial SK channels using pharmacological SK channels openers reduces mitochondrial ROS production, reversing RyR2 hyperoxidation, thereby attenuating pro-arrhythmic spontaneous SR Ca2+ release. We also found that SK1 subtype is functionally dead in rodent atrial myocytes, but it exhibits normal behavior in human cells, making SK1 an attractive atria-specific target to treat atrial fibrillation.  We conclude that   pharmacological enhancement of mitochondrial channels, including SK1, may provide strong therapeutic potential for treatment of atrial arrhythmias in cardiac diseases associated with gain of RyR2 function.

Type 2 diabetes (T2D) happens when the body's insulin-producing cells (called β-cells) struggle to release enough insulin, essential for controlling blood sugar levels. Normally, β-cells release a tiny fraction of their stored insulin in response to sugar (glucose) in the blood. This release is carefully balanced to meet the body’s needs while preventing dangerous insulin surges. Scientists are trying to understand how β-cells regulate insulin secretion, especially how they stop releasing too much insulin. One key discovery involves a protein called C1ql3, made and released by β-cells. C1ql3 seems to act as a "brake," slowing down insulin release in response to signals from the same β-cells that made it—a process called autocrine regulation. Research in mice has shown that when C1ql3 is explicitly removed from β-cells, insulin secretion increases in response to high glucose levels, improving blood sugar control. Similar findings were observed when blocking C1ql3’s interaction with its receptor, called BAI3, which is also found in β-cells. This suggests that C1ql3 and BAI3 work together to limit insulin release under certain conditions. In people with obesity or prediabetes (a state called impaired glucose tolerance, or IGT), β-cells make and release more C1ql3. This excess seems to interfere with insulin release, contributing to β-cell dysfunction and making it harder to control blood sugar levels. Even in human diabetes, high levels of C1ql3 are linked to reduced insulin secretion. Blocking the effects of C1ql3 could be a promising approach to boost insulin secretion and improve β-cell function in people with T2D, especially those who do not respond well to existing treatments like GLP-1 receptor agonists. This research highlights how understanding the complex regulation of insulin release can lead to better therapies for diabetes.

Our research focused on understanding how a specific protein called KRAS, which is often overactive in pancreatic cancer, interacts with other molecules to drive cancer growth. We wanted to explore if KRAS activates a second protein called PIP5K1A, which then produces molecules that feed back and further stimulate KRAS, creating a cycle that keeps the cancer cells growing.

Here’s what we discovered:

Key Protein Interactions
We found that PIP5K1A interacts with KRAS and other related proteins in cancer cells. This connection seems to happen through specific parts of these proteins that are common across different types of cancer-related proteins. This suggests that the interaction is crucial for the activity of KRAS.

New Cancer Treatments in Development
Working with another research team, we used advanced computer tools to identify new drugs that could block PIP5K1A and potentially stop the cancer growth. We have created 20 promising drug candidates, which we are now testing in cancer cells to see how well they work.

Testing in Cancer Models
After a lot of effort, we successfully created cancer cells that no longer produce PIP5K1A. We will test these cells in mice to see if removing PIP5K1A can slow down or stop tumor growth. This will help us understand if targeting PIP5K1A is a good strategy for treating pancreatic cancer.

Broader Findings
We also discovered that KRAS interacts with other similar molecules that play a role in cell growth. This suggests that KRAS is part of a bigger network of interactions that help cancer cells survive and spread.

New Methods to Study Cancer
We tested a new technique to track how molecules related to KRAS move inside cancer cells. This method showed us that KRAS is closely linked with certain fats in the cell, which are important for its cancer-driving activity.

Overall, our findings reveal new ways that KRAS keeps cancer cells alive, and we’ve identified promising new drugs that could potentially block this process. These discoveries could lead to better treatments for pancreatic cancer in the future.

This project aimed to investigate the cellular localization and function of trace amine-associated receptor 2 (TAAR2), which is an understudied GPCR. We used both cultured cells and rat brain as model systems.

Using a heterologous expression system, we found that TAAR2 was localized on the plasma membrane, cytosol, Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum in neuroblastoma cells. Upon agonist stimulation, TAAR2 translocated to the plasma membrane within 5-10 min. Interestingly, we also noticed a translocation of TAAR2 towards Golgi following 5-10 min agonist treatment whereas ER localization was reduced within the same time frame. The functional significance of Golgi-ER translocation warrants further investigation.  Moreover, TAAR2 was predicted to be coupled to Gs proteins and increase cAMP production upon agonist treatment. However, we did not see agonist-induced cAMP production upon agonist treatment in 5 min interval. These data suggest that TAAR2 may not couple to Gs or the stimulation by agonist is too transient to be detected. Treatments with short intervals (1 min) should be examined. 

Using rat brain and RNAscope, we examined Taar2 expression in a brain region and cell type-specific manner. We also included Taar1 in the RNAscope experiment as a comparison. In general, Taar2 expression was much lower than Taar1 expression in almost all the brain regions examined. Despite that the literature suggest a potential role of Taar2 in dopamine neuron activity, Taar2 mRNA levels in dopaminergic neurons were also low. Surprisingly, we found that Taar2 was moderately expressed in acetylcholinergic neurons in the striatum. How Taar2 regulates acetylcholinergic neuron activity should be investigated in the future.

This research project uncovered important insights into how the molecule 20-HETE and its receptor, GPR75, contribute to obesity and liver disease. Recently, reports have show that humans that are deficient in GPR75 are protected from obesity and exhibited a lower incidence of liver disease. Therefore, we took on this research to uncover how the activation of GPR75 via 20-HETE can drive these diseases and the array of signaling pathways that are influenced by GPR75. In mice fed a high-fat diet, those with normal GPR75 and elevated 20-HETE developed severe liver damage, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, and obesity. In contrast, mice lacking GPR75 were largely protected from these issues, even when their 20-HETE levels were high. Our studies revealed that 20-HETE activates a pathway through GPR75 that increases fat buildup in liver cells and favors fat uptake and storage. Interestingly, blocking GPR75 or removing it entirely prevented these effects. Instead it promoted the breakdown of fat for energy. Our studies using liver sells that have diminished GPR75 revealed improved activity of the mitochondria, the cell’s energy centers, which are critical for burning fat and generating energy. Interestingly, we observed that our water soluble GPR75 receptor blocker could significant prevent 20-HETE from activating GPR75 in liver cells, preventing harmful amount of lipid accumulation and inflammation. These findings suggest that GPR75 plays a key role in liver health and could be a promising target for treating obesity-related liver disease. Our future studies look to uncover more pathways and mechanisms that are influenced by GPR75 and we look to further characterize the therapeutic benefits associated with the GPR75 receptor blocker as we look to ultimately have a tool to fight disease.

Small secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) enable communication between cells, thereby regulating physiological processes and propagation of pathological conditions including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. A single cell can release multiple distinct EV subpopulations, each with specific content enrichment and functionality. Questions remain regarding how cargoes are enriched into EVs to foster this heterogeneity and how EV release is regulated. The primary cilium, a specialized organelle that protrudes from most eukaryotic cells, transmits signals by EV shedding. We use C. elegans that express fluorescently-tagged calcium homeostasis modulator (CLHM-1) and TRP polycystin-2 (PKD-2) ion channel EV cargoes to visualize EVs released from sensory neuron cilia. 

The most abundant phosphoinositide in the plasma membrane, phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), is concentrated in the ciliary base, but absent from the cilium proper. Since PI(4,5)P2 has been shown to impact protein localization, actin dynamics, endocytosis, exocytosis and membrane deformation, we reasoned that the ciliary compartmentalization of PI(4,5)P2 could have functional relevance for EV biogenesis. We discovered that the C. elegans type I phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate 5-kinase (PIP5K1) PPK-1 localizes to and regulates PI(4,5)P2 abundance in the ciliary base, while the C. elegans phosphoinositide 5-phosphatase INPP-1, localizes to and impacts PI(4,5)P2 levels in the cilium proper. Using a genetic approach to manipulate PI(4,5)P2 in ciliary compartments of C. elegans expressing fluorescently labeled EV cargoes, we showed for the first time that PI(4,5)P2 levels  impact shedding of EVs from sensory cilia. We discovered that PI(4,5)P2 had differential impact on two EV subpopulations, increasing shedding of EVs derived from the cilium tip, but reducing EV biogenesis from the ciliary base. Notably, this change in EV shedding did not affect cilium length or morphology, suggesting that this instead changes signaling. In addition, we found that PI(4,5)P2 levels also impact the movement and internalization of ciliary ion channels, demonstrating that the enzymes that control PI(4,5)P2 levels are global regulators of cilia biology.

The outcome of this R03 award has been the overexpression and purification of very large quantities of properly folded and fully functional Kv1.6 channel. Persistent drawbacks of heterologous protein expression systems like proteolysis, aggregation, misfolding and low yield continue to inhibit the biochemical characterization of understudied proteins. The Kv1.6 channel is considered an understudied protein that requires the investment of resources to produce a much needed systematic functional and structural characterization.
As leading regulators of K+ homeostasis in excitable cells throughout the CNS, voltage-gated potassium channels are attractive therapeutic targets with sensitivity to ligand binding and links to human disease. Nevertheless, despite advances using bacterial host systems and naturally derived fusion tags, modern-day overexpression and purification protocols remain largely insufficient to produce the high amounts of properly folded, functional protein required for structural-functional characterization. The present report explains our achievements developing a novel overexpression and purification protocol that employs a Denovo Expression Enhancer Protein (DEEP) to overexpress and purify the under-studied human voltage-gated potassium channel Kv1.6. Our data show the success of our DEEP sequence as a fusion partner for the overexpression and purification of Kv1.6 to a quantity and quality amenable for structural, functional, and pharmacological studies. We are in the process to start pursuing the structural determination of Kv1.6 by Cryo electron microscopy and single particle reconstruction. Additionally, we are in a vantage point to pursue the thermodynamic assessment of the ion binding properties of this ion channel as well as a functional characterization of the recombinant protein by electrophysiology in lipid bilayers of know lipid composition.

During the grant a spectrum a research reagents was generated and will be distributed to the broader research community through the Addgene plasmid depository.
We have produced methodologies to synthetical make CAMKV in a variety of forms for further research studies. Similarly, reagents for the study of protein protein interaction studies involving CAMKV were produced. We have also gained detailed insights into the behavior of CAMKV under in-vitro conditions and are using this knowledge for the further study of the biological function of CAMKV.

The goal of this proposal was to determine the ability of known HCAR1 ligands to promote complex formation between purified HCAR1 and G proteins or camelid single-chain antibody fragments (nanobodies). This work is significant because it will provide insight into the molecular pharmacology of HCAR1 ligands and the G protein coupling specificity of HCAR1, as well as identify multiple nanobodies stabilizing distinct conformations of HCAR1 which can be used to interrogate HCAR1 function. However, due to personnel issues, work on this project was halted and the award funds were not expended.

The overarching goal of this study was to identify and validate Pregnancy Upregulated Non-Ubiquitous CaM Kinase (PNCK) as a novel therapeutic target for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) by exploring its biological functions and developing potential inhibitors for future drug development. PNCK is a kinase that has been linked to RCC progression, poor patient outcomes, and aggressive disease features.
For Aim 1, RNA sequencing was performed on two RCC cell lines (Caki1 and 786-O) after PNCK was knocked down, revealing changes in the expression of various genes and shifts in key cellular pathways. Initial analyses revealed upregulated immune pathways such as interferon responses and TNF-alpha signaling, suggesting potential anti-tumor effects through increased immune surveillance. Additionally, pathways related to estrogen response and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) were downregulated, implying a reduction in tumor aggressiveness. The inhibition of hypoxia and TGF-beta signaling suggested a diminished potential for metastasis. While the 786-O cell line did not produce significant changes, Caki1 demonstrated strong evidence that PNCK knockdown affects important tumor survival mechanisms.
To further explore the impact of PNCK knockdown, Active Kinome Profiling identified 300 proteins whose levels changed in response, reflecting broader shifts in cell signaling networks. Among these proteins were MET, EGFR, FGFR, and TGFB2, all of which are linked to tumor growth and metastasis. The analysis also revealed the suppression of tumor-suppressive pathways like Wnt/β-catenin and Hippo signaling, suggesting PNCK’s involvement in promoting RCC proliferation and survival.
For Aim 2, the study focused on investigating PNCK inhibitors, identifying 176 unique compounds, and performing computational studies to refine binding models. Molecular dynamics simulations and analog searches were used to explore new chemical spaces, leading to the design of novel chemotypes. These are currently being prioritized  with selected inhibitors set to undergo target engagement studies.
In conclusion, this study has provided further insights into PNCK’s role in RCC, both as a driver of tumor survival and as a promising therapeutic target. RNA sequencing and kinome profiling have helped to map the signaling networks influenced by PNCK, while the ongoing optimization of inhibitors holds promise for future drug development. Together, these findings provide strong support for the development of selective PNCK inhibitors as a potential treatment strategy for RCC.

This study demonstrated that reduced expression of the lipid kinases PIP5K1A and PIP5K1B reduces viability of both mouse and human cancer cells. Immunofluorescent staining and immunoblotting found that knockdown of the PIP5K’s reduced PIP2 levels and active AKT, pointing to a possible mechanism for the lowered viability in cells with reduced expression of these lipid kinases.  We confirmed a reported Kras dependency to PIP5K1A in human cancer cells. We also found a novel dependency between PIP5K1B reduction and PTEN mutation across several human cancer cell lines. Approximately 13.5% of human cancers harbor a PTEN mutation and targeting PIP5K1B may be a new treatment strategy for these cancers.

Adhesion G protein-coupled receptors (aGPCRs) are crucial signaling proteins that allow cells to communicate, adapt, and respond to their environment. One member of this family, ADGRB3, is active in the brain and other tissues and has been linked to conditions such as cancer, psychiatric disorders, and muscle disease. Yet, how protein ligands or cellular forces switch on ADGRB3, and how its signaling is regulated, has remained poorly understood.
In this project, we found that a key region of ADGRB3 can assemble into clusters on its own and that it binds to ligand proteins in a calcium-dependent manner. We also identified natural variants of these ligand proteins that may influence how ADGRB3 signals in different cellular contexts. In addition, we obtained early structural data showing how these interactions occur and began building models that will guide future molecular and structural studies.
To achieve this, we developed new experimental strategies to biochemically and biophysically analyze ADGRB3 and its protein complexes. These approaches provided the first structural views of ADGRB3 interactions and established methods that can now be applied to larger and more physiologically relevant assemblies.
While some aspects of the project remain ongoing, the work has already produced important resources, preliminary data, and innovative strategies that will enable the generation of more complete models of ADGRB3 function. The results are being prepared for publication and will provide a foundation for future research on the role of ADGRB3 in health and disease. Ultimately, this knowledge may guide the development of new therapeutic strategies for conditions where ADGRB3 plays a role.

In the past one-year funding period, we worked on characterizing ADGRB3, an adhesion G-protein coupled receptor that is important for many different physiological systems in the body, including wiring of the brain. We studied the protein structure of the purified extracellular domain in solution and in a membrane environment, and determined the minimal binding region required to associate with its known binding partners, soluble synaptic proteins C1qLs. ADGRB3 and C1qLs play an important role during synapse formation and through the generous funding from the Common Fund Program “Illuminating the Druggable Genome” (IDG), for which we are very grateful, we were able to make substantial progress in our endeavors towards understanding ADGRB3:C1qL binding and the underlying molecular mechanism how they likely function in the body. This includes initial low-resolution cryo-EM reconstructions for both ADGRB3 and C1qL and we aim to use our data to apply for further research funding to illuminate these important molecules and their interactions through our comprehensive biophysical, biochemical and structural approaches. We expect that our research focused on ADGRB3 and C1qLs will be supported by other funding mechanisms such as the R01 program, since we have moved our understanding substantially forward, especially in regard to the mechanism. Furthermore, we are continuing to characterize extracellular and intracellular binding partners of ADGRB3. Our pilot grant also supported the training of Biochemistry graduate student Mr. Onyeka Obidi in advanced biophysical, biochemical, and structural methods and thanks to the opportunities created through this award, he is on track to graduation.

This pilot one-year award has provided support for the initial investigations regarding adck2 in the myocyte. Here, we investigated the role of this protein in cardiac myocytes in the presence of glucose and/or palmitate. The cardiac myocyte utilizes “flexible” metabolic fuels, and this flexibility is altered in various cardiac pathologies. This project has provided the basis for future studies that will further conceptualize the nature of this protein in myocardial biology and cardiac diseases. This has tremendous importance and potential impact for future pharmacological targets and drug design strategies to treat diseases.

This award allowed us to asses the role of PKR1 and PKR2 in the regulation of food intake. We demonstrated, using new mouse models, that, unlike previously thought, the anorexigenic effect of PK2 was mediated through PKR2 rather than PKR1. Additionally, we established that the site of action of PK2 was not the hypothalamus but rather the amygdala. This work identifies PKR2 in the amygdala, and more specifically the central nucleus of the amygdala, as an important regulator of the energy homeostasis machinery and a new promising target for the treatment of obesity.

T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation triggers a rise in intracellular Ca2+ critical for many T cell functions and immune responses. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCC or CaV) have been reported to regulate Ca2+ signaling and the function of T cells. Still, their mode of activation and role in electrically non-excitable T cells remains elusive. We identified the auxiliary CaV beta 1 subunit, encoded by the gene Cacnb1, as a regulator of T cell function by using an shRNA screen for ion channels and transporters expressed in immune cells. Cacnb1 was required for clonal T cell expansion after lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection. Deletion of Cacnb1 in T cells increased apoptosis, whereas proliferation, cytokine production, and Ca2+ signaling were unaffected. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology and Ca2+ recordings to detect VGCC activity, we could not detect voltage-gated Ca2+ currents or Ca2+ influx in human and mouse T cells upon depolarization with or without prior TCR stimulation. Deletion of stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1), previously shown to inhibit the L-type VGCC CaV1.2 in leukemic T cells, failed to reveal voltage-gated Ca2+ influx in primary T cells. Transcripts of several alpha 1 pore subunits of VGCCs can be detected in human (CaV3.3, CaV3.2) and mouse (CaV2.1) T cells. Still, exon usage analysis showed that the most 5' exons of these genes are not transcribed, likely resulting in N-terminally truncated and non-functional proteins. Our findings demonstrate that although CaV beta 1 regulates T cell survival and expansion, these effects are independent of VGCC channel function.

The result of this proposal is the establishment of TSSK6 as an anti-cancer target for tumors. Our work demonstrates that this kinase is essential to the growth of tumor cells. In addition, this grant established key tools for further study of the TSSK6 signaling network in cancer and sperm cells.

To fulfill our aims and characterize the role of the understudied protein kinase BCKDK in neurodevelopmental disorders, we generated a mouse model that overexpresses a tagged version of the kinase. Our studies were delayed due to the impact of COVID-19 on research operations. We are in the process of validating the model and testing its relevance to disease. Future studies using this mouse model will shed light on the function of BCKDK in the brain and link its overexpression to disease.

This proposal focused on identifying new ligands for understudied “pharmacologically dark” G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and on developing a new technology called PAM-scanning for expediting GPCR structural studies. Both approaches relied on novel applications of our CRISPR-based genome-editing technologies for studying human GPCRs in yeast. Through our ligand profiling experiments, we successfully identified new metabolite ligands for several dark GPCRs: HCAR3, GPR4, GPR65, and GPR68. A major finding was that kynurenic acid, a metabolite of the tryptophan pathway associated with inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, is a potent agonist of HCAR3. This finding has opened several potential new avenues of exploration for drug development at the interface of GPCR signaling, inflammation, and immunology. In addition to our ligand discovery efforts, we developed and applied our PAM-scanning technology that enables us to insert proteins that are crystallographic aids or functional reporters throughout GPCR structures in a high-throughput, unbiased manner. A major goal of the project was to use PAM-scanning to design functional GPCR chimeras for structural studies. Although we demonstrated proof-of-concept for our PAM-scanning technology, none of the many chimeras we engineered were functional. As a result, we are pivoting our PAM-scanning technology for use in other applications, including our efforts to address the current SARS-CoV2 pandemic.

This project was part of the Illuminating the Druggable Genome initiative, which aims to better understand poorly studied proteins belonging to families that have been successful targets for drug development. Protein kinases in particular include targets of nearly 100 FDA approved drugs. Our research focused on a protein kinase called TLK2 that is known to be involved in cell division and has been proposed as a potential cancer drug target. Protein kinases are enzymes that phosphorylate other proteins and thereby impact their cellular functions. Cells have thousands of distinct proteins, but protein kinases specifically target only a small number of these. TLK2 phosphorylates a protein called ASF1 whose function is to assist in the packaging of DNA into chromosomes. The research performed under this award revealed how TLK2 selectively phosphorylates ASF1 and not other proteins. We first identified amino acid sequences in ASF1 near its site of phosphorylation that promoted TLK2 kinase activity. We then systematically examined the capacity of TLK2 fragments to bind ASF1 to map the site of interaction. Using X-ray crystallography, we solved the three-dimensional structure of this fragment of TLK2 bound to ASF1. This analysis helps us to understand better how TLK2 works in cells, and may assist in the discovery of additional TLK2 substrate proteins. Finally, identification of this binding site offers a potential strategy for interfering with the TLK2-ASF1 interaction in cells using small molecules that could be developed into a new class of kinase inhibitor therapeutics.

The goal of our proposal has been to uncover the function and regulation of the understudied kinase protein kinase C (PKC) θ (theta) in order to better understand how to appropriately target it in disease. PKCθ, encoded by the gene PRKCQ, is a Ca2+-independent member of the seven gene family of diacylglycerol-dependent PKC isozymes that is selectively expressed in hematopoietic cells. The protein kinase C family was inappropriately targeted as an oncogene, resulting in three decades of failed clinical trials using PKC inhibitors to treat various cancers. Recent evidence has reframed this family of enzymes as generally participating in tumor suppressive functions. In this project, we combined bioinformatics, computational, biochemical, and cellular approaches to understand the molecular details of PKCθ and how disease-associated mutations impact function and biology. We developed a unifying model for the tertiary structure of protein kinase C isoymes, including PKCθ, which allowed us to identify surfaces that mediate autoinhibition.  We validated the model biochemically and showed that cancer-associated mutations in PKCθ predicated to perturb autoinhibition result in unrestrained activity of the kinase.  However, these constitutively active mutants are unstable such that they are paradoxically loss-of-function. This suggest that as with other protein kinase C isozymes, cancer-associated mutations in PKCθ are generally loss-of-function.

Variations in the genes that encode voltage-gated Ca2+ (Cav) channels are associated with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Among these is CACNA2D4,a gene encoding an extracellular Cav channel subunit (a2d-4) expressed in both the brain and retina. In the case of the retina, it has been established that a2d-4 is required for normal vision. In the brain, by contrast, its role remains understudied; we know neither the neural circuits in which it operates, nor what functions it may have there. The failure to address these questions has resulted in a bottleneck in our progress toward understanding how genetic alterations in this Cav channel contribute to the complex etiology of neuropsychiatric disorders.
The overall objective of the proposed research is to establish the cellular distribution of a2d-4 in the mouse brain and which behaviors are disrupted in mice lacking this protein. Our central hypothesis is that a2d-4 plays an essential role in regulating both cognitive and affective functions that are disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders. Using a2d-4 knockout (KO) mice, we obtained results that largely support this hypothesis. Compared to their wild-type (WT) littermates, a2d-4 KO mice exhibit defects in sensorimotor gating in prepulse inhibition assays as well as an anti-depressant phenotype in forced swim tests. While they showed no evidence of anxiety-like behavior or defects in motor behavior and coordination, a2d-4 KO mice were significantly more active than their WT counterparts. Considering that hyperactivity and impaired sensorimotor gating are features of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, our results suggest a role for a2d-4 in regulating cognitive and motor phenotypes associated with these disorders. 
We used quantitative PCR to determine the expression levels of a2d-4 in specific mouse brain regions. We found that while a2d-4 is expressed at much lower levels in the brain than in the retina, it is expressed at significant levels in areas regulating cognitive and motor function, including the hippocampus, striatum, cerebellum, and prefrontal cortex. Interestingly, we found that a2d-4 is expressed at extremely high levels in the pineal gland, a tissue that has been linked to the pathophysiology of various neuropsychiatric disorders. Collectively our results provide the first insights into the function of a2d4 in neural circuits outside of the retina, and how they may be disrupted in the context of neuropsychiatric disorders.

When the levels of glucose in the blood fall, the body activates a nervous reflex called the “counter-regulatory response”. This unconscious reflex restores the appropriate levels of glucose in the blood. The response is important because if it fails, hypoglycemia (a low glucose level) is not reversed, and this can lead to coma and even death. Hypoglycemia can occur in many ways. It can occur as a consequence of fasting. However, it is also frequently experienced by people with type I diabetes. An important part of the counter-regulatory response is the secretion of epinephrine from the adrenal gland. This hormone acts on the liver which in response, releases glucose into the blood. Because the adrenal is important in the counter-regulatory response we have been investigating how the secretion of epinephrine is controlled. We have previously found that two proteins (called Y2 and Y5) that are also made by the adrenal control how much epinephrine is secreted. In this study we asked which cells in the adrenal make the Y2 and Y5 proteins and how they are able to alter the secretion of epinephrine. 

The main findings of our work are:

•	The Y2 and Y5 proteins are made by the same cells that secrete the hormone epinephrine.
•	The Y2 and Y5 proteins rapidly inhibit the ability of the adrenal gland to synthesize epinephrine.

Our experiments used adrenal glands from mice, however the secretion of the hormone epinephrine from the human adrenal gland is likely to use the same mechanisms and proteins. The results of our work may help other scientists design drugs that can prevent hypoglycemia in people with type I diabetes.

We previously discovered that the understudied human protein RIOK3 is important during the early cellular responses to infection with Rift Valley fever virus.  The research funded by this R03 grant helped us begin to determine how RIOK3 elicits and regulates cellular antiviral response. We developed tractable assays of the biological function(s) of RIOK3 that will constitute important tools to accelerate research on this kinase.  Furthermore, we determined that active, full-length RIOK3 plays a key role in the production of antiviral cytokines, especially when a particular cellular viral receptor (RIG-I) is specifically activated.  Overexpression of the N-terminal portion of the protein had a negative impact on cytokine production, and enhancement of alternative splicing, which yields an mRNA transcript encoding only the N-terminal portion of the protein, also strongly suppressed production of cytokines.

We also determined that RIOK3 likely has several interacting partners that belong to different innate immune pathways.  To begin to filter the results from this complex immune landscape, we developed assays to specifically stimulate different innate immune response pathways.  We found that RIOK3’s strongest observable effects were on the RIG-I initiated pathway, indicating a direct or indirect interaction between RIOK3 and RIG-I.  We also developed a collaboration with Drs. Ben Major and Dhaval Bhatt at Washington University St. Louis to determine the binding partners of RIOK3 via a Biotin Ligation Proximity Assay.  In this collaboration, we have already obtained a list of about 20 potential binding partners for RIOK3 in unstimulated cells.  For this exciting collaboration, in April 2022 we sent samples of cells in an antiviral state to send to WUSTL for analysis of RIOK3 binding partners when activated.  We are still awaiting the results of this large experiment.

Thus, the funding has led to new insights into how the protein RIOK3 helps to mediate effective responses to viral infection, and has provided meaningful leads for further research in this exciting new realm.

Protein kinases (PKs) serve as biological switches in every cell. They constantly turn on and off key regulatory pathways, and slight perturbations in their function, too fast or too slow, can cause many diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and cardiac disorders. Fundamental learning and motor function are controlled by PKs, and many neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Parkinson’s Disease (PD) and Lou Gehrig’s Disease (ALS) are driven or made worse by defects in protein phosphorylation. PKs initiate the biological switch by transferring a single phosphate from a small molecule, ATP, to a protein substrate. There are over 500 PKs in human cells, and most are associated with diseases where a single amino acid change causes the process to be too fast or too slow. PKs also need to be precisely targeted to specific sites in each cell. If the PK is not at the right place, such as at mitochondria, and close to its substrate, it cannot function properly, and this can cause disease.
	One of the most important and abundant PKs, expressed in every human cell, is cAMP-dependent protein kinase or PKA. When you secrete adrenaline into your blood stream, for example, this neurotransmitter binds to the outside of many cells and triggers the synthesis of a small molecule inside the cell, cylic AMP (cAMP), and this “second messenger” causes a biological response. In a muscle cell, for example, cAMP triggers the release of glucose from the stored glycogen, a source of energy that can be rapidly mobilized. This is the classic “Fight or Flight” response. Memory and fear are all triggered by cAMP and PKA in brain. 
	PKA was the second PK to be discovered in 1968 and the first to be crystallized by Taylor at UCSD in 1991. This showed us the “kinase fold” which is conserved in every PK. The human kinome encodes for over 500 PKs, and although each share this same fold, all are regulated and localized in highly specific ways. Understanding the mechanism for activation and regulation of each kinase requires a multi-disciplinary approach. Crystallography shows us the structure and fold, but we also need to understand how and where each PK is expressed and localized in every tissue. Mutations that cause human disease are a treasure chest for scientists as they tell us which specific residues are important. For example, which mutation in PKA causes cancer, or Cushing’s Disease, or cardiac dysfunction and neuro-degeneration?
	PKA consists of two subunits - a catalytic protein kinase subunit (C-subunit) and a Regulatory (R) subunit that has cAMP binding sites. In the absence of cAMP the R-subunits trap the C-subunits in an inactive state that is unleashed when cAMP is synthesized in response to a particular hormone or neurotransmitter such as adrenalin. There are 4 functionally non-redundant R-subunits, and all localize differently and are activated in response to specific extracellular signals. The structure and localization of the R-subunits have been studied extensively, and much of this work has been led by the Taylor lab. There are two C-subunit isoforms, and almost everything we know about PKA signaling relates to the C subunit. Amazingly, the C subunit remains virtually unexplored even though 50% of PKA in brain is C. It is at the bottom of the “Dark Kinome” that includes important but still uncharacterized PKs. In contrast, C is at the top of the “Illuminated Kinome” and in many ways is the poster child of the PK superfamily. This IDG program (Illuminating the Druggable Genome) was launched as an attempt to stimulate studies on some of these important proteins that will almost certainly be drug targets and important for disease. Our goals were to build on our knowledge of PKA signaling to characterize the C subunit. C is especially important but also challenging because it has quite a few splice variants at the N-terminus, and we hypothesized that each splice variant, even though they differ by only a few amino acids, are likely to target and function differently. Our goals were to purify and characterize several C subunits and to show how they are localized in tissues. We also wanted to identify specific proteins that bind to the the C isoforms. Finally, and completely unanticipated, we learned of four novel C mutations in different patients around the world who had severe defects in cardiac and neural development. Until then very few disease mutations had been associated with C, but these patients showed very clearly that C and C were functionally non-redundant which was one of our fundamental hypothesis. By characterizing these C mutants we validated our hypothesis and provided new mechanistic understanding of C signaling. 
	We purified two C isoforms and formed holoenzyme complexes with two R-subunits.  In this way we established fundamental differences between the two isoforms and also between C and C. These proteins have also been set up for crystallization, and these structures will provide new opportunities for drug discovery. We also showed with purified proteins how function was impaired in the disease mutants. Basically these mutants were unable to interact properly with the different R-subunits and with another small protein in cells, PKI, that also inhibits the C-subunit in a cAMP-independent manner. These studies are opening new doors in our understanding of neuro-development and of PKA function in learning and memory. 
	In parallel with our structure studies, we used isoform-specific antibodies that recognize PKA isoforms in fixed tissues. Here we are using the retina as a model system that serves as a “Window into the Brain”. With the retina we show that C and C, like RI and RII in brain, also target to different cells and to different parts of each cell. Antibodies do not distinguish the C isoforms because their sequences are too similar so to identify which of the cells express each C isoform we designed small RNA probes that could distinguish between the messenger RNAs that code for each C isoform. In this way we can show clearly that C1 and C4ab localize to different cells and to different organelles. These tools now pave the way for us to characterize retinas and brains from AD patients and to explore the effects of aging and diet on PKA signaling in brain and other tissues such as liver and kidney. It is a new toolbox that we will make available to the entire signaling community. 
	With our purified proteins we are now also poised to engineer some additional tools such as nanobodies, which can distinguish the different C isoforms. These will be important tools for biochemists and cell biologists who study PKA signaling in different tissues but will also be valuable for searching for biomarkers in urine and plasma that may provide information about the early onset of diseases such as AD and diabetes. We are especially interested to screen under-represented populations such as African and Native Americans who are especially prone to kidney disease and diabetes. 
	This RO3 grant funded by the IDG initiative has opened a new frontier for PKA signaling. So much has been done over the past 50 years since the discovery of PKA, but we now appreciate that half of the PKA that is expressed had barely been studied at all. Furthermore, our preliminary work has established that C and C are not functionally redundant. Each is important for the development of tissues such as the heart and the brain. Teasing apart those differences, especially those that cause major disease, will take some time, but with the work funded under this pilot grant we have not only validated our fundamental hypothesis that C and C are different and each important as drivers for disease but we are also providing a tool box for new ways of experimentally characterizing these important proteins at the chemical, structural, and tissue level. We have laid a new foundation for exploring this as yet untapped world of PKA signaling.
